input.question: What is the security intent of CCoP 2.0's password and passphrase management requirement (Clause 5.9.2(b)), and how does CCoP 2.0 treat password length?

key_facts.fact: Default passwords must be changed and passwords/passphrases stored in hashed form
CCoP 2.0 prescribes no password complexity/length in the Code; length is deferred to industry standards such as NIST
Credential controls aim to prevent unauthorised access by raising the cost of credential attacks

ground_truth.expected_response: CCoP 2.0 Clause 5.9.2(b) requires that default passwords be changed and that passwords and passphrases be stored in their hashed forms. CCoP 2.0 does not prescribe password complexity or a minimum length in the Code itself; per Response to Feedback 11.28 it defers password length to industry standards such as NIST. The security intent of these credential controls (together with 5.1.2 authorisation/authentication and 5.7.2(b) multi-factor authentication) is to prevent unauthorised access by raising the cost of credential attacks such as brute-force and dictionary attacks. Reference: CCoP 2.0 5.9.2(b), 5.1.2, 5.7.2(b); Response to Feedback 11.28.
reasoning_chain: Locate the actual password/passphrase control in CCoP 2.0 (Clause 5.9.2(b))
Note CCoP prescribes no complexity/length rule and defers length to NIST (Response to Feedback 11.28)
State the security intent: change defaults and hash storage to raise the cost of credential attacks

forbidden_claims: Stating control purpose incorrectly for password complexity - preventing brute force
Confusing control mechanism with control intent
Attributing wrong security objectives to the control
The security intent or objective of the control
How the control achieves its security purpose
The threat or risk the control addresses
hallucination_patterns: Inventing intent not aligned with CCoP 2.0 principles
